lessons.title: Ante-mortem inspection of pigs
lessons.html:
Pigs in the lairage

Pigs are sensitive to heat and stress. Inspect them soon after arrival, at rest and while moving, as required by the Meat Safety Act 40 of 2000. Pigs that are stressed or overheated give pale, soft and watery meat.

What to look for

  • Skin: red diamond-shaped patches (a sign of erysipelas), red or purple discolouration of ears and belly, bite and fight wounds, mange.
  • Breathing: coughing, open-mouth breathing, panting from heat stress.
  • Movement: lameness, swollen joints, pigs that cannot stand.
  • Body: ruptures (hernias), swellings, abscesses, tail-bite wounds.
  • Behaviour: dullness, fever, trembling or nervous signs.

Notifiable disease

African swine fever and classical swine fever are serious notifiable diseases in South Africa. Signs can include high fever, red-purple skin, weakness and sudden deaths in a batch. If you suspect them, stop slaughter of that batch, isolate the pigs, report to the veterinarian immediately and follow biosecurity rules so the disease does not spread on trucks, boots or equipment.

Handling and welfare

Pigs must have water and, in hot weather, cooling by water sprays where the lairage provides them. Move pigs in small groups using boards. Never kick or beat pigs. Mixing strange pigs causes fighting and skin damage, so keep groups from the same farm together. The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 applies to all handling.

Your safety

Boars and sows can bite. Use a pig board between you and the pig and never put your hand near a pig's mouth.

lessons.title: Head and offal inspection of pigs
lessons.html:
The head

Pig heads usually stay attached to the carcass until inspection. Inspect:

  • Submandibular lymph nodes: incise and look for abscesses and tuberculosis-type lesions. Pigs can carry mycobacterial lesions in the head nodes.
  • Cheek (masseter) muscles and tongue: incise the cheek muscles and examine the tongue for pork measles (Cysticercus cellulosae), the cyst stage of the human tapeworm Taenia solium.
  • Throat and tonsils: look for inflammation and abscesses.

Why pork measles matters

Pork measles is a public health risk in parts of South Africa where pigs roam freely and people do not have proper toilets. If people swallow the tapeworm eggs, the cysts can develop in their own body, including the brain, causing epilepsy. This is why careful inspection and correct judgement are so important. Infected carcasses are detained for the veterinarian and judged according to the regulations.

Red offal

  • Lungs: view and palpate for pneumonia, pleurisy and abscesses. Lungs that took in scalding water are condemned.
  • Heart: view, open and incise for measles cysts and inflammation of the heart sac.
  • Liver: view and palpate. White scars called milk spots are caused by migrating roundworm larvae. Badly spotted livers are condemned.
  • Spleen and kidneys: look for swelling and small dark red spots, which may point to a fever or septic condition.

Green offal

View stomach and intestines and the mesenteric lymph nodes. Look for inflammation, ulcers and abscesses. Intestines that are torn and spill content contaminate the carcass, which must be trimmed.

lessons.title: Carcass inspection and judgement of pigs
lessons.html:
Inspecting the pig carcass

Pigs are usually scalded and dehaired, so the skin stays on and must be inspected carefully.

  • Skin: erysipelas diamonds, bruises, fight and tail-bite wounds, mange, scalding damage and left-over hair.
  • Muscles: cut surfaces of the diaphragm and other exposed muscle for measles cysts. Look for pale, soft, watery meat that comes from stress.
  • Inner surfaces: pleurisy (lungs stuck to the chest wall), peritonitis and abscesses, including in the spine after tail biting.
  • Joints: swollen joints may point to arthritis or erysipelas.
  • Smell: a strong urine-like smell in carcasses of entire boars (boar taint) is a quality defect handled according to procedure.

Judgement examples

FindingUsual action
Local tail-bite abscessTrim the affected area; check the spine for spread
Pleurisy on one sideStrip the affected lining; pass the rest
Milk spot liverCondemn the liver
Pork measles cystsDetain for the veterinarian; judged according to the regulations
Acute erysipelas with fever signsDetain; often total condemnation
Suspected swine feverStop, isolate, report immediately

Records and feedback

Record condemnations by producer. Feedback on measles, tail biting, pneumonia and milk spots helps farmers improve housing, deworming and hygiene. Report notifiable diseases without delay.

Key points

  • Check pig skin for erysipelas diamonds and red-purple discolouration.
  • Suspected African swine fever: stop, isolate and report immediately.
  • Incise the cheek muscles and check tongue and heart for pork measles.
  • Pork measles is a serious human health risk; detain affected carcasses.
  • Milk spot livers are caused by roundworm larvae and are condemned.
